title: Bell nonlocality with directly generated telecom-band spin-photon entanglement
authors: Dong-Yu Huang, Jian Wang, Xiao-Long Zhou, Ze-Min Shen, Si-Jian He, Qi-Yang Huang, Yi-Jia Liu, Yu-Shu Chen, Quan Jiang, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo
abstract: Quantum nonlocality, typically revealed through entanglement distribution across quantum networks, is a cornerstone of quantum information science. Long-distance distribution of entanglement requires the information carrier, i.e. flying photons, to operate in the minimum-loss telecom band of optical fiber. While extensive efforts have been devoted to the direct generation of entanglement between C-band telecom photons and various stationary spins, the verification of quantum nonlocality remains an outstanding challenge. Here, utilizing a dipole transition in rubidium atoms with a wavelength of 1530 nm and a cavity-assisted protocol, we achieve resonant excitation and direct emission of C-band telecom photons from a single atom, generating spin-photon entanglement with a measured Bell state fidelity exceeding 91.4%. We then verify Bell nonlocality by observing a Bell inequality violation of 2.455(77) > 2 using this high-quality entangled pair. These results extend the wavelength of a single-atom quantum emitter to the telecom C-band, achieving sufficiently high-fidelity spin-photon entanglement to finally verify Bell nonlocality. This work thereby provides a promising building block for a large-scale atom-based quantum network capable of distributed quantum metrology and long-distance quantum communication.
summary: The research demonstrates the direct generation of spin-photon entanglement in the telecom C-band using a single Rubidium atom coupled to an optical cavity. By achieving high fidelity and violating a Bell inequality, the authors successfully verified quantum nonlocality, paving the way for scalable, long-distance quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge is verifying quantum nonlocality using entanglement distributed via photons, which necessitates operating in the low-loss telecom C-band for long-distance quantum networks.
main_result: The authors successfully generated spin-photon entanglement with fidelity exceeding 91.4% and verified Bell nonlocality by observing a violation of the CHSH inequality ($2.455(77) > 2$).
method: They utilized a cavity-assisted protocol involving resonant excitation in a single Rubidium atom to directly emit telecom C-band photons entangled with the atomic spin state.
model_or_system: The system uses a single $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atom trapped within a fiber-based Fabry-Pérot micro-cavity. The entanglement is generated via a cascaded dipole transition, coupling the atomic spin qubit to the emitted telecom photon.
key_observables: Bell state fidelity (> 91.4%), Bell inequality violation ($S > 2$), and coincidence counts between 1530 nm and 780 nm photons.
important_parameters: Telecom C-band (1530 nm), Rubidium transition wavelengths, Rabi frequencies ($\Omega_{ge} \approx 60 	ext{ MHz}$), and the CHSH parameter value.
main_assumptions: The overall heralded detection efficiency for the telecom photon is limited by various optical losses in the collection path.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (trapping, cavities, multiple laser sources) and time-domain measurements showing coincidence counts between the entangled photons and heralming signals.
paper_structure: The paper details the complex engineering required for atomic trapping and state preparation (MOT $ightarrow$ optical tweezer), followed by the specific protocol for two-photon excitation to generate entanglement, culminating in Bell test measurements.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in quantum networking: generating high-fidelity entangled qubits at telecom wavelengths using solid-state or atomic emitters, providing a crucial building block for distributed quantum information protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic diagram of the experimental setup. An optical tweezer traps the atom at the center of the FFPC. A magnetic field of 170 mG is applied along the z direction as a quantization axis. The emitted telecom photons are collected by one of the aspherical lenses placed along the quantization axis. For entanglement characterization, they are directed through a subsequent polarization analysis module and are detected by a two-channel superconducting nanowire single photon detector (SNSPD). The spectral filtering setup of the photons is omitted for clarity.
